script.opening: (Friendly, matter-of-fact, a little impatient.) "Morning. Bit of a non-event this, I think — the blood donor place turned me away because my iron was low and told me to see you. I feel completely fine, never better. Can you just give me some iron tablets to top me up so I can get back to donating? I've given 60-odd times, I don't want to stop now over nothing."

facts.text: Feels well. If pushed, a bit more tired on his walks, "but I'm 61". No breathlessness, chest pain or dizziness.

If asked: "Now you mention it, a bit looser than they used to be. A few months, maybe. I put it down to getting older." Going twice a day instead of once. "No blood. Maybe a bit darker now and then. I wouldn't call it black."
"No, none of that. Stomach's fine." No indigestion, heartburn, trouble swallowing, vomiting or abdominal pain.
"Not that I've noticed. I haven't weighed myself." Appetite normal.
"Ibuprofen for my knees. Most days, if I'm honest" — bought over the counter, 400 mg once or twice a day for a couple of years. No aspirin or blood thinners. No allergies.
"Yes, I eat pretty well. Nothing unusual" — meat most days, not vegetarian.
"Not that I know of" — no bowel cancer or coeliac disease in the family he knows about.
Retired postman, married, walks the dog twice a day. Ex-smoker (stopped at 40). Drinks about 10 units a week. Donates blood every 16 weeks; last successful donation was 4 months ago.

Cheerful and a bit dismissive. Give the bowel change and darker stools only when asked about bowels. If asked what he thinks is going on: "Honestly? That I've given too much blood and I need topping up. Though it did rattle me a bit, being sent away." If the doctor mentions bowel cancer: "A growth? You mean cancer? I feel fine." Then sensible: "Fair enough. I'd rather know." If simply given iron, take it and leave happy (the trap).

ice.ideas: "I've given too much blood over the years — I just need topping up."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — being a donor is part of who he is ("I'd rather be the one giving"); he doesn't like being a patient. Being turned away rattled him more than he lets on.

cues: "Bit of a non-event." — playing it down.
"It did rattle me a bit, being sent away." — the quiet worry, if asked.
"I'd rather be the one giving." — his identity as a donor.

checkpoints.text: OWNS the incidental result — does not accept "I feel fine / it’s a non-event" — and confirms/characterises it as iron-deficiency anaemia (low Hb, low MCV, low ferritin)
Knows the core rule: iron-deficiency anaemia in a MAN (or postmenopausal woman) is GI blood loss / malignancy until proven otherwise — because men do not menstruate, the iron loss must be sourced

Takes a targeted GI history (bowel-habit change, rectal bleeding/dark stools, weight loss, abdominal pain, dyspepsia/dysphagia, family history, NSAID/anticoagulant use, diet) and treats the darker stools/looser habit as positive cues

Applies NICE HTG690 and NICE NG12: OFFERS FIT (≥10 µg Hb/g → suspected cancer pathway colorectal referral; a low FIT with strong concern does not delay referral), and arranges BIDIRECTIONAL endoscopy (OGD + colonoscopy, BSG 2021) for unexplained IDA, plus coeliac serology (anti-tTG)
Reviews the regular IBUPROFEN as a contributor (PPI/stop) WITHOUT assuming it is the whole cause, and gives iron replacement ALONGSIDE investigation — never instead of it
Honours his donor identity and the wish to resume, while being honest that the finding needs investigation first — and does NOT collude with "just top me up and clear me to donate"
Explains clearly why a man who feels well still needs urgent tests — making the reasoning understandable and respectful rather than alarmist or dismissive

Safety-nets and follows up: arranges FIT/referral/endoscopy with clear timing, advises red flags (rectal bleeding, weight loss, worsening symptoms), explains the donation question will follow the results, confirms understanding, and books review — owns the result, never iron-and-wave-off

worked.txt: "I can see why it feels like a fuss when you feel so well — but I’m actually really glad the blood service flagged this, and I don’t think it’s a non-event. Low iron in a man is something we always look into properly, even when, especially when, you feel fine."

"Here’s my honest reasoning. Women can lose iron through periods; men don’t. So if your iron is low, it’s being lost somewhere, and the commonest place is slowly from the bowel — often without you ever seeing blood. Most causes are harmless, but one we have to rule out is a growth in the bowel that bleeds quietly."

"You mentioned your stools have been a bit darker now and then, and your bowels a touch looser for a few months. Those are exactly the things I need to act on. And the ibuprofen for your knees can irritate the stomach — it might be playing a part, but I can’t assume it’s the whole story."

"So: I’m doing a stool test called FIT that looks for hidden blood, a coeliac blood test, and — given your age and symptoms — I’m referring you on the urgent pathway to have a camera test at both ends, the stomach and the bowel, to find where the iron’s going. I’ll start you on iron tablets at the same time, but to fix it, not to dodge finding the cause."

worked.lbl: Honour the donor, hold the line
worked.txt: "On donating — I genuinely respect that you’ve given 60 times, that’s remarkable. The honest answer is we sort out why your iron is low first; getting you healthy is how you get back to donating safely, not the other way round."

"If you see fresh blood, your stools turn black and tarry, you lose weight without trying, or you feel unwell, contact us sooner. I’ll get the tests and referral moving today, and we’ll go through every result together — including what it means for donating."

f.learning: The incidental-findings principle: a result generated by another service (here, a blood-donation deferral for a low haemoglobin) lands with the GP, who now OWNS the duty to act — "I feel fine / it’s a non-event" must be resisted, and the finding worked up as if the patient had presented with symptoms. Confirmed iron-deficiency anaemia (low Hb, low MCV, low ferritin) in a MAN of any age, or in any postmenopausal woman, is gastrointestinal blood loss / malignancy until proven otherwise — because men do not menstruate, the lost iron must be sourced — commonly a right-sided colorectal cancer (which bleeds occultly and presents with anaemia, not visible bleeding), gastric cancer, or benign causes (NSAID gastropathy, angiodysplasia, coeliac). NICE HTG690: offer quantitative FIT in adults with IDA, and NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026): FIT ≥10 µg Hb/g → suspected cancer pathway colorectal referral (FIT now guides the referral; a low FIT does not close the case if concern persists); investigate BOTH ends with bidirectional endoscopy (OGD + colonoscopy; BSG 2021) for unexplained IDA; and check coeliac serology (anti-tTG). Review regular NSAID use as a contributor WITHOUT assuming it is the whole story (it can coexist with cancer), and give iron replacement alongside — never instead of — investigation, since replacing iron and sending him back to donate masks the cause and delays diagnosis. Honour the proud-donor identity while holding the line that investigation precedes any return to donation, take the targeted GI history (treating darker stools and bowel-habit change as positive cues), and safety-net and follow up.

knowledge.guideline: NICE HTG690 (2023, formerly DG56) — FIT in primary care · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · BSG iron-deficiency anaemia guideline (2021) · NICE NG20 (2015) — coeliac disease · BNF (NSAIDs, oral iron)
knowledge.summary: Iron-deficiency anaemia in a 61-year-old man is gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, however well he feels. The GP owns a result another service found: FIT, coeliac serology, lower and upper GI investigation, an NSAID review, and iron alongside — not instead of — investigation.

points.t: A result from the blood service is now the GP’s to act on. Feeling well does not change the work-up: a confirmed iron-deficiency anaemia gets the same investigation as if he had come in with symptoms.

points.h: Men don’t lose iron without a reason
points.t: BSG 2021: in men and postmenopausal women with iron-deficiency anaemia, gastroscopy and colonoscopy are the first-line GI investigations. Right-sided colon cancer often bleeds invisibly and presents as anaemia. Regular donation can contribute to low iron, but it is not an explanation to accept without investigation.

points.h: FIT and the NICE NG12 threshold
points.t: NICE HTG690 recommends quantitative FIT to guide referral in adults with iron-deficiency anaemia or a change in bowel habit. NICE NG12: refer on a suspected cancer pathway for colorectal cancer if FIT is at least 10 µg Hb/g faeces. A low FIT does not close the case in unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia — the upper GI tract still needs looking at, and HTG690 says not to delay referral if strong clinical concern persists.
BSG 2021: screen adults with iron-deficiency anaemia for coeliac disease. NICE NG20: IgA tTG with total IgA as first choice, while he is still eating gluten.

Regular NSAIDs cause GI blood loss and ulcers (BNF). Review it, offer alternatives for the knees, and consider a PPI if an NSAID must continue — but never let the NSAID become the whole explanation; it can coexist with a cancer.

BSG 2021: one tablet of oral iron once daily (alternate days if not tolerated); product and strength per BNF. Recheck the FBC within about 4 weeks. Warn that iron darkens stools — and note that his darker stools came before any iron. Black, tarry stools with dizziness or collapse need same-day assessment.

dg.d: Open question about the letter; did not jump to prescribing iron; noted “non-event” and the donor pride.
Donor identity, dislike of being a patient, what donating means to him, practical impact of endoscopy.
FIT; coeliac serology (IgA tTG with total IgA); urgent lower and upper GI endoscopy; in-person examination, weight and FBC recheck on iron.
Colorectal or gastric cancer vs NSAID gastropathy vs coeliac vs angiodysplasia vs donation-related iron loss vs dietary.
Asked about bleeding, melaena, weight loss, dysphagia, family history; recognised IDA in a man as GI loss until proven otherwise (BSG 2021; NICE NG12).
Confirmed iron-deficiency anaemia of GI origin until proven otherwise, with bowel-habit change as a positive cue.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: FIT and urgent referral for bidirectional endoscopy; iron alongside; stop ibuprofen with an alternative; donation decision follows the results.
NSAID stopped or gastroprotected; knee pain managed; coeliac excluded; iron response checked.
Same-day symptoms (tarry stools, dizziness, fresh blood); 999 for collapse or haematemesis; in-person review this week; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up looser stools, darker stools and daily ibuprofen, and the fact that being deferred rattled him.
Idea (given too much blood, needs topping up); concern (being made a patient, losing his donor role); expectation (iron and clearance to donate).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — being a donor is part of who he is ("I'd rather be the one giving"); he doesn't like being a patient. Being turned away rattled him more than he lets on — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Morning Mr Aldous, I’m Dr Lee. Can you see and hear me all right? … Good. You’ve had a letter from the blood service — tell me what’s happened.
model.why: Checks the video and opens with his account

model.text: Bit of a non-event, I think. They turned me away because my iron was low and told me to see you. I feel completely fine. Can you just give me some iron tablets so I can get back to donating? I’ve given 60-odd times — I don’t want to stop over nothing.

Sixty donations is a real achievement, and I can hear how much it matters to you. I do want to talk about iron. I’d also like to understand why it’s low, because that’s what gets you back to donating safely. Can I ask some questions first, then we’ll agree a plan?
model.why: Honours the donor identity and sets an agenda that includes the cause

model.text: Fair enough. Fire away.
The repeat test we did confirms your iron is low and it’s affecting your blood count. Have you noticed any change in your bowels over the last few months?
model.why: Owns the result and starts the targeted GI history

model.text: Now you mention it, a bit looser than they used to be. A few months, maybe. I put it down to getting older.
And the colour of your stools — any blood, or have they looked darker or black?
model.why: Asks about rectal bleeding and melaena

model.text: No blood. Maybe a bit darker now and then. I wouldn’t call it black.
That’s helpful — I’ll come back to that. Any tummy pain, indigestion, heartburn or trouble swallowing?
model.why: Screens upper GI symptoms

model.text: No, none of that. Stomach’s fine.
Have you lost any weight without trying, or noticed your appetite change?
model.why: Asks about weight loss without assuming the answer

model.text: Not that I’ve noticed. I haven’t weighed myself.
We can check that when you come in. Do you take anything for pain, or any blood thinners?
model.why: Medicine history — NSAIDs and anticoagulants

model.text: Ibuprofen for my knees. Most days, if I’m honest.
Thank you. And your diet — do you eat a reasonable range of food?
model.why: Excludes dietary deficiency as the whole story

model.text: Yes, I eat pretty well. Nothing unusual.
And has anyone in your family had bowel cancer or other bowel problems?
model.why: Family history

model.text: Not that I know of.
What did you think when the letter said your iron was low?
model.why: Explores his idea behind “non-event”

model.text: Honestly? That I’ve given too much blood and I need topping up. Though it did rattle me a bit, being sent away.
That sounds like it knocked you more than you’ve let on. Is there anything about it that’s worried you?
model.why: Picks up the cue that he was unsettled

model.text: I suppose I just don’t like being a patient. I’d rather be the one giving.

That makes sense. Can I be honest with you about my thinking? Women can lose iron through periods; men don’t. So when a man’s iron is low, we need to find where it’s going — and the commonest place is slowly from the gut, often without any visible blood. Most causes are harmless, like an irritated stomach from ibuprofen. But one we must rule out is a growth in the bowel that bleeds quietly.
model.why: Explains why IDA in a man means GI loss until proven otherwise

model.text: A growth? You mean cancer? I feel fine.

I know, and I’m not saying you have cancer. Bowel problems that cause anaemia often don’t make people feel ill at first — that’s exactly why the blood service flagging this is useful. Your looser bowels and slightly darker stools are things I have to take seriously alongside the low iron.
model.why: Holds honesty and reassurance together; links his cues to the plan

model.text: Right. So what happens?

Here’s what I suggest. A stool test called FIT, which looks for hidden blood. A blood test for coeliac disease, which can stop you absorbing iron — keep eating bread and pasta as normal until it’s done. And I’m referring you on the urgent pathway for camera tests of your bowel and your stomach, to find the source.
model.why: FIT, coeliac serology and urgent bidirectional endoscopy

model.text: Both ends? That sounds like a lot.
It is two tests, often on the same day, with sedation offered. They tell us far more than any blood test. The urgent pathway aims to have an answer within about four weeks.
model.why: Explains what to expect in plain language

model.text: And the iron?

I’ll start you on iron tablets today — one a day — to rebuild your blood, alongside the tests, not instead of them. They’ll turn your stools dark or black, so if they become tarry and sticky, or you feel faint, ring us that day.
model.why: Iron alongside investigation and warns about stool colour

model.text: The ibuprofen is probably not helping — it can make the stomach bleed. Would you be willing to stop it and try a gel on the knees, or paracetamol, while we sort this out?
model.why: Reviews the NSAID without blaming it for everything

model.text: I can try the gel.
And donating — I respect that it matters to you. The blood service will decide when you can go back once we know the cause and your iron is recovered. Getting you well is the route back.
model.why: Does not collude with “clear me to donate”

model.text: Fair enough. I’d rather know.

If you notice fresh blood, black tarry stools, feel dizzy or faint, get breathless or lose weight without trying, contact us the same day. If you collapse or vomit blood, call 999. I’d like to see you in person this week to examine you, weigh you and do the bloods, and I’ll go through every result with you.
model.why: Specific safety-net and follow-up

model.text: Okay. Not what I came in for, but I get it.
Just so I know I’ve explained it well — if someone at home asks what the doctor said, what will you tell them?
model.why: Teach-back

model.text: That men shouldn’t be low on iron, so they’re checking my bowel and stomach with a camera, a stool test and a coeliac test. Iron tablets meanwhile, gel instead of ibuprofen, and no donating till it’s sorted.
Spot on. You did the right thing coming in. Anything else before we finish?
model.why: Closes and shares the floor

model.text: No. Thanks, doctor.

social.t: Decades of donating can be central to how someone sees themselves. Being turned away can feel like a loss; framing investigation as the route back engages rather than threatens.
“I don’t like being a patient” can mean missed appointments. Explain what the tests involve and what to expect so he stays on the pathway.

legal.t: If he has sedation for endoscopy he must not drive home and needs someone to collect him; the unit will say how long to avoid driving. No DVLA notification is needed for the investigation itself.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): act on results you receive. A blood-service letter is a clinical result; document the plan, the referral and his agreement.
Prescribing iron without investigating the cause falls short of good clinical care. Iron and investigation go together.

community.t: Bowel Cancer UK and Guts UK for information on FIT and endoscopy; NHS Blood and Transplant for questions about returning to donate once cleared.

redFlags: Change to looser stools over months and occasional darker stools — act on them
Black, tarry stools with dizziness or collapse, or haematemesis — same-day or emergency
Weight loss, dysphagia, upper abdominal pain — upper GI criteria in NICE NG12
psychosocial: Dislikes being a patient; mild avoidance
Knee pain that drives daily ibuprofen
ice: Idea: “I’ve given too much blood and just need topping up”
Concern: being made a patient; being turned away rattled him
Expectation: iron tablets and clearance to donate

playbook.diagnosis: Confirmed iron-deficiency anaemia in a 61-year-old man with looser stools for months, occasional darker stools and daily ibuprofen. GI blood loss until proven otherwise — colorectal or gastric cancer must be excluded, alongside NSAID-related bleeding and coeliac disease.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your blood is short of iron. Women can lose iron through periods; men don’t. So in a man, low iron usually means a small amount of blood is slowly being lost somewhere in the gut, often without you seeing it. Most causes are harmless, but we have to find it — that’s what the tests are for.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought you’d just given too much blood, and you’d like to get back to donating. I want that too — and finding out why your iron is low is how we get you there safely.”
management.psychosocial: Use his donor identity as the motivation: investigation is the route back. Explain the tests plainly so he doesn’t drop out of the pathway.
sharedPlan: FIT; coeliac serology (IgA tTG with total IgA) while eating gluten; urgent referral for colonoscopy and gastroscopy
Oral iron once daily alongside investigation; recheck FBC in about 4 weeks
Stop ibuprofen; topical NSAID gel or paracetamol for the knees; PPI if an oral NSAID is unavoidable
Return to donation decided by the blood service after the cause is found and treated
safetyNet: Same day: black tarry stools, fresh blood, dizziness, faintness or breathlessness; 999 for collapse or vomiting blood
In-person review this week (examination, weight, bloods); GP goes through all results with him

pitfalls.intro: Everyone knows iron-deficiency anaemia in a man needs investigating. This station is failed when a pleasant, well patient talks the doctor into the quick fix, or when the doctor explains the risk so bluntly that the patient disengages.

items.fail: Prescribing iron and telling him to return to donating.
items.why: Treats the number, masks occult bleeding and can delay a colorectal cancer diagnosis by months — a clear clinical-management fail.
items.fix: Iron alongside, never instead of, FIT and bidirectional endoscopy.

items.fail: Blaming the ibuprofen or the donations and stopping there.
items.why: Both can contribute, but neither excludes a cancer. BSG 2021 still recommends upper and lower GI investigation in men with IDA.
items.fix: “The ibuprofen may be part of it, but I can’t assume it’s the whole story.”

items.fail: Relying on a negative FIT to avoid referral.
items.why: In unexplained IDA a low FIT does not exclude an upper GI source, and NICE HTG690 says not to delay referral if concern persists.
items.fix: Arrange FIT and refer for bidirectional endoscopy; the FIT result supports rather than replaces the plan.

items.why: Coeliac disease is a common, treatable cause of IDA (BSG 2021; NICE NG20).
items.fix: IgA tTG with total IgA while he is still eating gluten.

items.fail: Brushing past “I don’t want to stop donating” as irrelevant.
items.why: It is his hidden agenda. Ignoring it loses rapport and risks him not attending.
items.fix: Acknowledge the 60 donations and frame investigation as the route back.

items.fail: Not warning that iron turns stools black.
items.why: He already reports darker stools. Without the warning, he can’t tell expected iron effect from melaena.
items.fix: “Iron makes stools dark; if they become tarry and sticky, or you feel faint, ring us that day.”

Bowel habit, blood, dark or black stools, weight, dyspepsia, swallowing, NSAIDs, anticoagulants, diet, family history.
He thinks he has given too much blood; being turned away rattled him; he dislikes being a patient.

Tarry stools, dizziness, fresh blood — same day; collapse — 999. See him in person this week. Donation follows the results. Teach-back.

wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains the “men don’t have periods” logic in words he repeats; turns his darker stools and looser habit into reasons rather than footnotes; warns that iron darkens stools; honours his donor identity while holding the line; picks up that being deferred rattled him; teach-back and an in-person review booked.

avoid.dont: “You’ve probably just donated too often — here’s some iron.”
avoid.instead: “Donating can lower iron, but in a man I always need to check the gut too — that’s how we make sure it’s safe.”
avoid.why: Accepting donation or NSAIDs as the cause is the trap that delays a bowel cancer diagnosis.

avoid.dont: “We need to rule out bowel cancer urgently.”
avoid.instead: “Most causes are harmless, but one we must rule out is a growth that bleeds quietly — the camera tests will tell us.”
avoid.why: Leading with cancer frightens and loses him; honest context keeps him on the pathway.

avoid.dont: “Once your iron’s back up you can donate again.”
avoid.instead: “The blood service will decide once we know the cause and you’ve recovered.”
avoid.why: Clearing him to donate before investigation colludes with the quick fix and is outside your role.

SCA_MODELS.text: Not that I’ve noticed. I haven’t weighed myself.
We can check that when you come in. Do you take anything for pain, or any blood thinners?
SCA_MODELS.why: Medicine history — NSAIDs and anticoagulants

SCA_MODELS.text: Ibuprofen for my knees. Most days, if I’m honest.
Thank you. And your diet — do you eat a reasonable range of food?
SCA_MODELS.why: Excludes dietary deficiency as the whole story

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, I eat pretty well. Nothing unusual.
And has anyone in your family had bowel cancer or other bowel problems?
SCA_MODELS.why: Family history

SCA_MODELS.text: Not that I know of.
What did you think when the letter said your iron was low?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores his idea behind “non-event”

SCA_MODELS.text: Honestly? That I’ve given too much blood and I need topping up. Though it did rattle me a bit, being sent away.
That sounds like it knocked you more than you’ve let on. Is there anything about it that’s worried you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Picks up the cue that he was unsettled

SCA_MODELS.text: I suppose I just don’t like being a patient. I’d rather be the one giving.

That makes sense. Can I be honest with you about my thinking? Women can lose iron through periods; men don’t. So when a man’s iron is low, we need to find where it’s going — and the commonest place is slowly from the gut, often without any visible blood. Most causes are harmless, like an irritated stomach from ibuprofen. But one we must rule out is a growth in the bowel that bleeds quietly.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains why IDA in a man means GI loss until proven otherwise

SCA_MODELS.text: A growth? You mean cancer? I feel fine.

I know, and I’m not saying you have cancer. Bowel problems that cause anaemia often don’t make people feel ill at first — that’s exactly why the blood service flagging this is useful. Your looser bowels and slightly darker stools are things I have to take seriously alongside the low iron.
SCA_MODELS.why: Holds honesty and reassurance together; links his cues to the plan

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. So what happens?

Here’s what I suggest. A stool test called FIT, which looks for hidden blood. A blood test for coeliac disease, which can stop you absorbing iron — keep eating bread and pasta as normal until it’s done. And I’m referring you on the urgent pathway for camera tests of your bowel and your stomach, to find the source.
SCA_MODELS.why: FIT, coeliac serology and urgent bidirectional endoscopy

SCA_MODELS.text: Both ends? That sounds like a lot.
It is two tests, often on the same day, with sedation offered. They tell us far more than any blood test. The urgent pathway aims to have an answer within about four weeks.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains what to expect in plain language

SCA_MODELS.text: And the iron?

I’ll start you on iron tablets today — one a day — to rebuild your blood, alongside the tests, not instead of them. They’ll turn your stools dark or black, so if they become tarry and sticky, or you feel faint, ring us that day.
SCA_MODELS.why: Iron alongside investigation and warns about stool colour

SCA_MODELS.text: The ibuprofen is probably not helping — it can make the stomach bleed. Would you be willing to stop it and try a gel on the knees, or paracetamol, while we sort this out?
SCA_MODELS.why: Reviews the NSAID without blaming it for everything

SCA_MODELS.text: I can try the gel.
And donating — I respect that it matters to you. The blood service will decide when you can go back once we know the cause and your iron is recovered. Getting you well is the route back.
SCA_MODELS.why: Does not collude with “clear me to donate”

SCA_MODELS.text: Fair enough. I’d rather know.

If you notice fresh blood, black tarry stools, feel dizzy or faint, get breathless or lose weight without trying, contact us the same day. If you collapse or vomit blood, call 999. I’d like to see you in person this week to examine you, weigh you and do the bloods, and I’ll go through every result with you.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net and follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. Not what I came in for, but I get it.
Just so I know I’ve explained it well — if someone at home asks what the doctor said, what will you tell them?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: That men shouldn’t be low on iron, so they’re checking my bowel and stomach with a camera, a stool test and a coeliac test. Iron tablets meanwhile, gel instead of ibuprofen, and no donating till it’s sorted.
Spot on. You did the right thing coming in. Anything else before we finish?
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes and shares the floor

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Thanks, doctor.

SCA_STEM.name: Geoffrey Aldous
SCA_STEM.recent: Letter from the blood donation service: deferred from donating because of low haemoglobin, advised to see GP. Repeat FBC arranged by the practice confirms iron-deficiency anaemia (low Hb, low MCV, low ferritin). No FIT or coeliac serology on record.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation to discuss his blood results and the donor letter.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE HTG690 (2023, formerly DG56) — FIT in primary care · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · BSG iron-deficiency anaemia guideline (2021) · NICE NG20 (2015) — coeliac disease · BNF (NSAIDs, oral iron)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Iron-deficiency anaemia in a 61-year-old man is gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, however well he feels. The GP owns a result another service found: FIT, coeliac serology, lower and upper GI investigation, an NSAID review, and iron alongside — not instead of — investigation.

points.t: A result from the blood service is now the GP’s to act on. Feeling well does not change the work-up: a confirmed iron-deficiency anaemia gets the same investigation as if he had come in with symptoms.

points.h: Men don’t lose iron without a reason
points.t: BSG 2021: in men and postmenopausal women with iron-deficiency anaemia, gastroscopy and colonoscopy are the first-line GI investigations. Right-sided colon cancer often bleeds invisibly and presents as anaemia. Regular donation can contribute to low iron, but it is not an explanation to accept without investigation.

points.h: FIT and the NICE NG12 threshold
points.t: NICE HTG690 recommends quantitative FIT to guide referral in adults with iron-deficiency anaemia or a change in bowel habit. NICE NG12: refer on a suspected cancer pathway for colorectal cancer if FIT is at least 10 µg Hb/g faeces. A low FIT does not close the case in unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia — the upper GI tract still needs looking at, and HTG690 says not to delay referral if strong clinical concern persists.
BSG 2021: screen adults with iron-deficiency anaemia for coeliac disease. NICE NG20: IgA tTG with total IgA as first choice, while he is still eating gluten.

Regular NSAIDs cause GI blood loss and ulcers (BNF). Review it, offer alternatives for the knees, and consider a PPI if an NSAID must continue — but never let the NSAID become the whole explanation; it can coexist with a cancer.

BSG 2021: one tablet of oral iron once daily (alternate days if not tolerated); product and strength per BNF. Recheck the FBC within about 4 weeks. Warn that iron darkens stools — and note that his darker stools came before any iron. Black, tarry stools with dizziness or collapse need same-day assessment.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question about the letter; did not jump to prescribing iron; noted “non-event” and the donor pride.
Donor identity, dislike of being a patient, what donating means to him, practical impact of endoscopy.
Picked up looser stools, darker stools and daily ibuprofen, and the fact that being deferred rattled him.
Idea (given too much blood, needs topping up); concern (being made a patient, losing his donor role); expectation (iron and clearance to donate).
FIT; coeliac serology (IgA tTG with total IgA); urgent lower and upper GI endoscopy; in-person examination, weight and FBC recheck on iron.
Colorectal or gastric cancer vs NSAID gastropathy vs coeliac vs angiodysplasia vs donation-related iron loss vs dietary.
Asked about bleeding, melaena, weight loss, dysphagia, family history; recognised IDA in a man as GI loss until proven otherwise (BSG 2021; NICE NG12).
Confirmed iron-deficiency anaemia of GI origin until proven otherwise, with bowel-habit change as a positive cue.
FIT and urgent referral for bidirectional endoscopy; iron alongside; stop ibuprofen with an alternative; donation decision follows the results.
NSAID stopped or gastroprotected; knee pain managed; coeliac excluded; iron response checked.
Same-day symptoms (tarry stools, dizziness, fresh blood); 999 for collapse or haematemesis; in-person review this week; teach-back.

social.t: Decades of donating can be central to how someone sees themselves. Being turned away can feel like a loss; framing investigation as the route back engages rather than threatens.
“I don’t like being a patient” can mean missed appointments. Explain what the tests involve and what to expect so he stays on the pathway.

legal.t: If he has sedation for endoscopy he must not drive home and needs someone to collect him; the unit will say how long to avoid driving. No DVLA notification is needed for the investigation itself.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): act on results you receive. A blood-service letter is a clinical result; document the plan, the referral and his agreement.
Prescribing iron without investigating the cause falls short of good clinical care. Iron and investigation go together.

community.t: Bowel Cancer UK and Guts UK for information on FIT and endoscopy; NHS Blood and Transplant for questions about returning to donate once cleared.

redFlags: Change to looser stools over months and occasional darker stools — act on them
Black, tarry stools with dizziness or collapse, or haematemesis — same-day or emergency
Weight loss, dysphagia, upper abdominal pain — upper GI criteria in NICE NG12
psychosocial: Dislikes being a patient; mild avoidance
Knee pain that drives daily ibuprofen
ice: Idea: “I’ve given too much blood and just need topping up”
Concern: being made a patient; being turned away rattled him
Expectation: iron tablets and clearance to donate

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Confirmed iron-deficiency anaemia in a 61-year-old man with looser stools for months, occasional darker stools and daily ibuprofen. GI blood loss until proven otherwise — colorectal or gastric cancer must be excluded, alongside NSAID-related bleeding and coeliac disease.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your blood is short of iron. Women can lose iron through periods; men don’t. So in a man, low iron usually means a small amount of blood is slowly being lost somewhere in the gut, often without you seeing it. Most causes are harmless, but we have to find it — that’s what the tests are for.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought you’d just given too much blood, and you’d like to get back to donating. I want that too — and finding out why your iron is low is how we get you there safely.”
management.psychosocial: Use his donor identity as the motivation: investigation is the route back. Explain the tests plainly so he doesn’t drop out of the pathway.
sharedPlan: FIT; coeliac serology (IgA tTG with total IgA) while eating gluten; urgent referral for colonoscopy and gastroscopy
Oral iron once daily alongside investigation; recheck FBC in about 4 weeks
Stop ibuprofen; topical NSAID gel or paracetamol for the knees; PPI if an oral NSAID is unavoidable
Return to donation decided by the blood service after the cause is found and treated
safetyNet: Same day: black tarry stools, fresh blood, dizziness, faintness or breathlessness; 999 for collapse or vomiting blood
In-person review this week (examination, weight, bloods); GP goes through all results with him

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Everyone knows iron-deficiency anaemia in a man needs investigating. This station is failed when a pleasant, well patient talks the doctor into the quick fix, or when the doctor explains the risk so bluntly that the patient disengages.

items.fail: Prescribing iron and telling him to return to donating.
items.why: Treats the number, masks occult bleeding and can delay a colorectal cancer diagnosis by months — a clear clinical-management fail.
items.fix: Iron alongside, never instead of, FIT and bidirectional endoscopy.

items.fail: Blaming the ibuprofen or the donations and stopping there.
items.why: Both can contribute, but neither excludes a cancer. BSG 2021 still recommends upper and lower GI investigation in men with IDA.
items.fix: “The ibuprofen may be part of it, but I can’t assume it’s the whole story.”

items.fail: Relying on a negative FIT to avoid referral.
items.why: In unexplained IDA a low FIT does not exclude an upper GI source, and NICE HTG690 says not to delay referral if concern persists.
items.fix: Arrange FIT and refer for bidirectional endoscopy; the FIT result supports rather than replaces the plan.

items.why: Coeliac disease is a common, treatable cause of IDA (BSG 2021; NICE NG20).
items.fix: IgA tTG with total IgA while he is still eating gluten.

items.fail: Brushing past “I don’t want to stop donating” as irrelevant.
items.why: It is his hidden agenda. Ignoring it loses rapport and risks him not attending.
items.fix: Acknowledge the 60 donations and frame investigation as the route back.

items.fail: Not warning that iron turns stools black.
items.why: He already reports darker stools. Without the warning, he can’t tell expected iron effect from melaena.
items.fix: “Iron makes stools dark; if they become tarry and sticky, or you feel faint, ring us that day.”
